Observed and expected count frequencies

Source: R/diagnostics.R
expected_counts.Rd

Compares how often each count value (0, 1, 2, ...) occurs in the data with how often the fitted model expects it to occur. The expected frequency of a value \(k\) is the sum over observations of the fitted probability \(P(Y_i = k)\). The row for \(k = 0\) shows whether the model predicts the right number of zeros.

Usage

expected_counts(object, max_count = NULL, ...)

Arguments

object

An nbreg or zinbreg fit.

max_count

Largest count to tabulate separately; larger counts are grouped in the last row. By default the largest observed count (with positive weight).

...

Not used (an error if supplied).

Value

A data frame with columns count (character: "0", "1", ..., and the grouped last row), observed and expected. It has max_count + 2 rows, and attributes max_count and total (the total weight).

Details

Frequencies are weighted by the prior weights, and observations with weight 0 are left out. So with frequency weights, the table is that of the expanded data. For the negative binomial (NB) model, \(P(Y_i = k)\) is the NB probability with mean \(\mu_i\) and the fitted theta. For the zero-inflated model it is \(\pi_i I(k = 0) + (1 - \pi_i) P_{NB}(k)\).

Counts above max_count are grouped in a last row labelled "<max_count + 1>+" (for example "11+" when max_count = 10). Its expected frequency is \(\sum_i w_i (1 - \pi_i) P_{NB}(Y_i > m)\), with \(m\) = max_count and \(\pi_i = 0\) for NB. Both columns therefore add up to the total weight.

The table needs one probability per observation and count value, so a computation of more than 1e8 probabilities (observations times max_count + 2) is refused before it starts.

Errors and warnings

  • nbzinbreg_error_input: object of the wrong class, max_count not NULL or a whole number of at least 0, a table of more than 1e8 probabilities, or unused arguments.

See also

rootogram(), predict.zinbreg()

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x = rnorm(200))
d$y <- ifelse(runif(200) < 0.3, 0, rnbinom(200, size = 2, mu = exp(1 + d$x)))
expected_counts(nbreg(y ~ x, data = d), max_count = 8)
#>    count observed  expected
#> 1      0       82 76.998365
#> 2      1       24 36.129677
#> 3      2       27 21.380280
#> 4      3       13 14.016844
#> 5      4        9  9.795681
#> 6      5        8  7.161659
#> 7      6        9  5.417780
#> 8      7        3  4.210826
#> 9      8        4  3.345759
#> 10    9+       21 21.543129
expected_counts(zinbreg(y ~ x | 1, data = d), max_count = 8)
#>    count observed  expected
#> 1      0       82 81.070675
#> 2      1       24 29.234405
#> 3      2       27 20.455340
#> 4      3       13 14.400810
#> 5      4        9 10.394218
#> 6      5        8  7.708353
#> 7      6        9  5.863975
#> 8      7        3  4.563993
#> 9      8        4  3.624145
#> 10    9+       21 22.684086
